source.text: וַתָּ֣שַׁר דְּבוֹרָ֔ה וּבָרָ֖ק בֶּן־אֲבִינֹ֑עַם בַּיּ֥וֹם הַה֖וּא לֵאמֹֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: And sang Deborah and Barak son of Abinoam on the day the that, saying,

en.L: And Deborah and Barak son of Abinoam sang on that day, saying:
en.B: That day Deborah and Barak son of Abinoam sang, and these were the words:
en.R: On that day Deborah and Barak, the son of Abinoam, sang this song:

decisions.choice: Deborah sang, and Barak with her: she leads the song
alternatives: Deborah and Barak sang together as equals
decisions.reason: The verb is singular and feminine, agreeing with Deborah, who is named first; Barak joins her. Exodus 15:1 has a singular verb with Moses in the same way, though the people sing with him.

decisions.choice: on that day: the day of the victory over Sisera told in chapter 4
decisions.reason: The song that follows (verses 2-31a) is a poem that retells the same battle. It celebrates what chapter 4 narrates, and adds details the story does not give, such as the storm (verses 4, 20-21) and the tribes that stayed away (verses 15-17).

decisions.choice: sang this song:
decisions.reason: "Saying" introduces the words that follow. Balanced and Readable name them as a song.

source.text: בִּפְרֹ֤עַ פְּרָעוֹת֙ בְּיִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל בְּהִתְנַדֵּ֖ב עָ֑ם בָּרֲכ֖וּ יְהוָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: In letting loose of locks in Israel, in offering themselves willingly of [the] people, bless Yahweh!

en.L: "When locks hung loose in Israel, \q when [the] people offered themselves willingly, \q bless {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}!
en.B: "When long hair hung loose in Israel, \q when the people volunteered freely, \q bless {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}!
en.R: "In Israel the fighters let their hair hang long, \q and the people gladly offered themselves for battle. \q Praise {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}!

decisions.choice: when locks of hair hung loose: the warriors left their hair uncut, a sign that they had given themselves to fight the LORD's war
alternatives: when the leaders took the lead in Israel
decisions.reason: The verb means "let loose" or "let go", and the noun is used for long uncut hair in Numbers 6:5 (the Nazirite's hair) and Deuteronomy 32:42 (the long-haired heads of the enemy). The other reading takes both words from a root found in related languages that means "be first" or "lead": "when the leaders took the lead in Israel". That would match the commanders of verse 9. The evidence is divided.

decisions.choice: offered themselves willingly: came forward to fight of their own free will
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used for freewill offerings (Exodus 35:29); here people give themselves. It returns in verse 9. Not every tribe came forward (verses 15-17).

decisions.choice: the two "when" clauses give the reason for praise; "bless the LORD" is a command to the hearers
decisions.reason: The command is plural. The song opens and returns (verse 9) with this call to praise the LORD for the people's readiness to fight.

decisions.choice: a double quotation mark opens here and closes at the end of the song in verse 31, before "And the land had peace"
decisions.reason: Verse 1 introduces the song as the words Deborah and Barak sang, so the whole poem is set as one quotation. Words quoted inside it (verses 23, 28, 30) take single quotes.

decisions.choice: fighters (Readable); for battle (Readable); praise (Readable)
decisions.reason: Readable says who let their hair hang loose and why the people offered themselves, as verses 8-9 and 13-18 make clear. Blessing God means praising him, so Readable says "praise".

source.text: שִׁמְע֣וּ מְלָכִ֔ים הַאֲזִ֖ינוּ רֹֽזְנִ֑ים אָֽנֹכִ֗י לַֽיהוָה֙ אָנֹכִ֣י אָשִׁ֔ירָה אֲזַמֵּ֕ר לַֽיהוָ֖ה אֱלֹהֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: Hear, kings; give ear, rulers; I to Yahweh, I will sing; I will make music to Yahweh, [the] God of Israel.

en.L: Hear, kings; give ear, rulers! \q I, to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, I will sing; \q I will make music to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel.
en.B: Listen, you kings; pay attention, you rulers! \q I will sing, I myself, to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}; \q I will make music to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel.
en.R: Listen, kings! Pay attention, rulers! \q I will sing to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. \q I will make music for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel.

decisions.choice: kings and rulers: the rulers of the nations, called to hear what Israel's God has done
decisions.reason: Foreign kings are summoned as witnesses, as the kings of Canaan were defeated (verse 19). The same pair of words appears in Psalm 2:2 and Proverbs 8:15.

decisions.choice: I, I: the singer says "I" twice for emphasis
decisions.reason: The pronoun is not needed with the verb, so repeating it stresses that the singer herself will praise the LORD, not the kings.

decisions.choice: make music: sing praise, often with instruments
decisions.reason: The verb is used for playing an instrument as well as singing praise (Psalm 33:2; 98:5).

source.text: יְהוָ֗ה בְּצֵאתְךָ֤ מִשֵּׂעִיר֙ בְּצַעְדְּךָ֙ מִשְּׂדֵ֣ה אֱד֔וֹם אֶ֣רֶץ רָעָ֔שָׁה גַּם־שָׁמַ֖יִם נָטָ֑פוּ גַּם־עָבִ֖ים נָ֥טְפוּ מָֽיִם׃

records.literal_gloss: Yahweh, in your going out from Seir, in your marching from [the] field of Edom, earth trembled, also heavens dripped, also clouds dripped water.

en.L: O {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, when {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} went out from Seir, \q when {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} marched from the field of Edom, \q [the] earth trembled, and [the] heavens dripped; \q yes, [the] clouds dripped water.
en.B: {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, when {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} set out from Seir, \q when {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} strode out from the land of Edom, \q the earth shook, the skies poured, \q the clouds poured down water.
en.R: {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} came out from Seir. \q You marched out from the land of Edom. \q Then the earth shook, and the sky poured rain. \q Water came pouring down from the clouds.

decisions.choice: Seir and Edom: the LORD comes from the mountains in the south, where he met Israel in the wilderness
decisions.reason: Seir is the mountain country of Edom, south of the Dead Sea. Other old poems picture the LORD coming from there as a warrior to help his people (Deuteronomy 33:2; Habakkuk 3:3; Psalm 68:8-9).

decisions.choice: the earth shook and the heavens poured rain: a great storm as the LORD comes
decisions.reason: The quaking earth and the pouring clouds picture the LORD's coming in storm. The rain explains how the Kishon swept the enemy away (verse 21) and why Sisera's chariots were no use (4:15).

decisions.choice: the land of Edom
decisions.reason: The word usually means a field; here it means the open country or territory of Edom.

decisions.choice: the sky poured rain
decisions.reason: The verb means "drip" or "pour"; Readable says what fell from the heavens.

source.text: הָרִ֥ים נָזְל֖וּ מִפְּנֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה זֶ֣ה סִינַ֔י מִפְּנֵ֕י יְהוָ֖ה אֱלֹהֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: Mountains quaked before Yahweh, this [one of] Sinai, before Yahweh, [the] God of Israel.

en.L: [The] mountains quaked before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, \q this [One] of Sinai, before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel.
en.B: The mountains quaked at the presence of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, \q the One of Sinai, at the presence of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel.
en.R: The mountains shook before {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, \q the God of Israel, the God who came to Mount Sinai.

decisions.choice: quaked: shook before the LORD
decisions.reason: As the vowels are written, the verb would mean "flowed", picturing the mountains streaming or melting. Read as the verb "quake", it says the mountains shook, as in Isaiah 63:19 and 64:2, and the ancient Greek translation reads "shook". Both picture the mountains overcome by the LORD's coming.

decisions.choice: the One of Sinai: a title of the LORD, the God who appeared at Sinai
decisions.reason: The short word "this" can work as "the one of" in old Hebrew poetry, and Psalm 68:9 uses the same phrase as a title of God. The other reading is "even Sinai": Sinai itself quaked before the LORD (Exodus 19:18).

decisions.choice: the God who came to Mount Sinai
decisions.reason: Readable explains the title: the LORD is known as the God who came down on Mount Sinai (Exodus 19:18-20).

source.text: בִּימֵ֞י שַׁמְגַּ֤ר בֶּן־עֲנָת֙ בִּימֵ֣י יָעֵ֔ל חָדְל֖וּ אֳרָח֑וֹת וְהֹלְכֵ֣י נְתִיב֔וֹת יֵלְכ֕וּ אֳרָח֖וֹת עֲקַלְקַלּֽוֹת׃

records.literal_gloss: In [the] days of Shamgar son of Anath, in [the] days of Jael, ceased roads, and walkers of paths walked roads winding.

en.L: In the days of Shamgar son of Anath, in the days of Jael, \q [the] roads ceased, \q and those walking the paths walked [by] winding roads.
en.B: In the time of Shamgar son of Anath, in the time of Jael, \q the highways lay empty, \q and travelers went by crooked side roads.
en.R: In the days of Shamgar son of Anath and in the days of Jael, \q no one traveled on the main roads. \q Anyone who had to go somewhere took winding back roads.

decisions.choice: Shamgar and Jael: the time just before the victory, when Canaan oppressed Israel
decisions.reason: Shamgar son of Anath fought the Philistines (3:31); Jael is the woman who killed Sisera (4:17-22; verses 24-27). The song dates the hard years by them.

decisions.choice: the roads ceased: the main roads were deserted
decisions.reason: With other vowels the same letters mean "caravans": "the caravans stopped". Either way, trade and travel had stopped because the roads were unsafe.

decisions.choice: those who had to travel used winding paths, to stay out of sight of raiders
decisions.reason: The contrast is between the open main roads and twisting byways where travelers could hide.

decisions.choice: lay empty (Balanced); no one traveled on (Readable)
decisions.reason: Roads "ceasing" means no one used them; Balanced and Readable say so.

source.text: חָדְל֧וּ פְרָז֛וֹן בְּיִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל חָדֵ֑לּוּ עַ֤ד שַׁקַּ֨מְתִּי֙ דְּבוֹרָ֔ה שַׁקַּ֥מְתִּי אֵ֖ם בְּיִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: Ceased villagers in Israel, they ceased, until that I arose, Deborah, that I arose, a mother in Israel.

en.L: [The] villagers ceased in Israel; they ceased, \q until I, Deborah, arose, \q [until] I arose, a mother in Israel.
en.B: The villages of Israel were deserted, deserted, \q until I, Deborah, arose, \q until I arose, a mother in Israel.
en.R: No one was left in the villages of Israel, no one, \q until I, Deborah, rose up, \q until I rose up like a mother for Israel.

decisions.choice: villagers: the people of open country villages; village life came to an end
decisions.reason: The word is related to the one for unwalled villages (Deuteronomy 3:5; Esther 9:19), so the line says the countryside was emptied, as the roads were (verse 6). Others take it as "warriors" or "leaders": "the warriors held back in Israel". The word comes again in verse 11.

decisions.choice: I arose: Deborah speaks of herself
decisions.reason: As the text is written, the verb is "I arose". The same ending was also an old form of "you" said to a woman, which gives "until you arose, Deborah"; verse 12 speaks to Deborah in the same way. The meaning is the same: the change came when Deborah stood up to lead.

decisions.choice: a mother in Israel: a leader who protects and cares for the people
decisions.reason: The title is used of a city that sustains its people in 2 Samuel 20:19. It honors Deborah as one who looked after Israel, not as the mother of children.

decisions.choice: the villages were deserted (Balanced); no one was left in the villages (Readable)
decisions.reason: The verb "ceased" means the village people were gone; Balanced and Readable say it of the villages.

source.text: יִבְחַר֙ אֱלֹהִ֣ים חֲדָשִׁ֔ים אָ֖ז לָחֶ֣ם שְׁעָרִ֑ים מָגֵ֤ן אִם־יֵֽרָאֶה֙ וָרֹ֔מַח בְּאַרְבָּעִ֥ים אֶ֖לֶף בְּיִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: He chose gods new; then war [was in the] gates; shield, if it was seen, and spear, among forty thousand in Israel?

en.L: [Israel] chose new gods; \q then war [was at the] gates. \q Was a shield seen, or a spear, \q among forty thousand in Israel?
en.B: Israel chose new gods; \q then war came to the city gates. \q Not a shield or spear was to be seen \q among forty thousand in Israel.
en.R: Israel chose to worship new gods, \q and then war came right up to the city gates. \q Not one shield or spear could be found \q among forty thousand in Israel.

decisions.choice: Israel chose new gods: the people turned to other gods, and war followed
decisions.reason: The verb is singular, with Israel (or each one) as its subject. The book says again and again that Israel turned to other gods and was then handed over to its enemies (2:11-14; 4:1-2), and Deuteronomy 32:17 speaks of "new gods". The line is very hard, and the ancient translations differ. Others read "God chose new leaders" or "when they chose new gods".

decisions.choice: war at the gates: the enemy fought right at the gates of Israel's towns
alternatives: then there was fighting in the gates
decisions.reason: The word for "war" is found only here and seems to mean fighting. The gates were where a town was defended. Some divide or change the letters to get other sense, such as "barley bread".

decisions.choice: "was a shield seen?": not one shield or spear was to be seen
decisions.reason: The words "if it was seen" have the force of a strong denial. Israel had no weapons to fight with, as later under the Philistines (1 Samuel 13:19-22).

decisions.choice: forty thousand
decisions.reason: On the size of numbers counted in "thousands", see the note at Numbers 1.

decisions.choice: Israel
decisions.reason: The verb has no named subject; Israel is the people the song speaks of.

source.text: לִבִּי֙ לְחוֹקְקֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל הַמִּֽתְנַדְּבִ֖ים בָּעָ֑ם בָּרֲכ֖וּ יְהוָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: My heart [is] to [the] commanders of Israel, the ones offering themselves willingly among the people; bless Yahweh!

en.L: My heart [is] toward the commanders of Israel, \q those offering themselves willingly among the people. \q Bless {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}!
en.B: My heart is with the commanders of Israel, \q who volunteered freely among the people. \q Bless {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}!
en.R: My heart is with Israel's commanders, \q who gladly came forward from among the people. \q Praise {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}!

decisions.choice: my heart is with: the singer's warm loyalty and admiration
decisions.reason: The heart stands for a person's will and affection; the singer gives her heart to those who came forward.

decisions.choice: commanders: those who give orders
decisions.reason: The word comes from a verb meaning "engrave, decree", and is used for a ruler who gives commands (Genesis 49:10; Deuteronomy 33:21). It returns in verse 14.

decisions.choice: who offered themselves willingly: as in verse 2
decisions.reason: The same verb as verse 2. The commanders themselves volunteered, and so did people with them.

decisions.choice: praise
decisions.reason: As in verse 2.

source.text: רֹכְבֵי֩ אֲתֹנ֨וֹת צְחֹר֜וֹת יֹשְׁבֵ֧י עַל־מִדִּ֛ין וְהֹלְכֵ֥י עַל־דֶּ֖רֶךְ שִֽׂיחוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: Riders of she-donkeys white, sitters on carpets, and walkers on [the] road, tell!

en.L: Riders of white she-donkeys, \q those sitting on saddle cloths, \q and walkers on the road, tell [of it]!
en.B: You who ride on white donkeys, \q you who sit on rich saddle cloths, \q and you who walk along the road, speak out!
en.R: You who ride white donkeys and sit on fine saddle cloths, \q and you who walk along the roads, tell the story!

decisions.choice: riders on white donkeys: the rich and the leaders
decisions.reason: Leaders and their families rode donkeys (10:4; 12:14). The color word is rare; it may mean white, or a pale reddish gray.

decisions.choice: those sitting on saddle cloths: riders seated on rugs or blankets
decisions.reason: The word seems to come from the one for a garment, so it means cloths spread to sit on, either on the saddle or at home. It is found only here, and some take it as a place name or as "in judgment".

decisions.choice: tell: everyone, from the rich who ride to those who walk, is called to tell what the LORD has done
decisions.reason: The command looks forward to verse 11, where the LORD's righteous acts are told at the watering places. The verb can mean "talk about", "think over" or "sing".

decisions.choice: tell [of it] (Literal); tell the story (Readable)
decisions.reason: The verb has no object; what is to be told is the story the song tells.

source.text: מִקּ֣וֹל מְחַֽצְצִ֗ים בֵּ֚ין מַשְׁאַבִּ֔ים שָׁ֤ם יְתַנּוּ֙ צִדְק֣וֹת יְהוָ֔ה צִדְקֹ֥ת פִּרְזֹנ֖וֹ בְּיִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל אָ֛ז יָרְד֥וּ לַשְּׁעָרִ֖ים עַם־יְהוָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: From [the] sound of [those] dividing between watering places, there they recount [the] righteous acts of Yahweh, [the] righteous acts of his villagers in Israel; then went down to the gates [the] people of Yahweh.

en.L: At [the] sound of [those] dividing [the flocks] between the watering places, \q there they recount the righteous acts of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, \q the righteous acts of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} villagers in Israel. \q Then the people of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} went down to the gates.
en.B: Over the voices of herders at the watering places, \q there they retell the righteous acts of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, \q the righteous acts of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} villagers in Israel. \q At that time the people of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} went down to their gates.
en.R: Listen to the shepherds talking at the wells. \q There they tell the right and saving things {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has done, \q what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has done for {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} village people in Israel. \q Then the people of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} went down to their town gates.

decisions.choice: the sound of those who divide the flocks at the watering places: herders at the wells, where people meet and talk
alternatives: at the sound of the archers
louder than the noise of the archers
to the sound of the singers
decisions.reason: The rare word comes from a verb meaning "divide", so it may mean those who share out water or divide the flocks at the wells. Others connect it with the word for arrows ("archers", the raiders who once made the wells unsafe) or take it as "singers". "From the sound" may also mean "louder than the sound". The line is very uncertain.

decisions.choice: the righteous acts of the LORD: his saving deeds for his people
decisions.reason: The plural of the word for righteousness names acts in which the LORD set things right by rescuing Israel (1 Samuel 12:7; Micah 6:5).

decisions.choice: his villagers: the LORD's people in the open villages
decisions.reason: The same word as verse 7. If it means "warriors" there, it means "his warriors" here.

decisions.choice: then the people of the LORD went down to the gates: they went back to their towns, or went down to fight at the gates
decisions.reason: The gates were a town's meeting place and its point of defense (verse 8). The line may mean that town life began again, or that the people went down to battle. It also leads into the call of verse 12.

decisions.choice: over the voices of herders
decisions.reason: Balanced takes "from the sound" as heard over the noise at the wells and names the herders.

decisions.choice: the right and saving things the LORD has done
decisions.reason: Readable explains "righteous acts": the LORD did what was right by saving his people.

source.text: עוּרִ֤י עוּרִי֙ דְּבוֹרָ֔ה ע֥וּרִי ע֖וּרִי דַּבְּרִי־שִׁ֑יר ק֥וּם בָּרָ֛ק וּֽשֲׁבֵ֥ה שֶׁבְיְךָ֖ בֶּן־אֲבִינֹֽעַם׃

records.literal_gloss: Awake, awake, Deborah! Awake, awake, speak a song! Arise, Barak, and take captive your captives, son of Abinoam!

en.L: Awake, awake, Deborah! \q Awake, awake, utter a song! \q Arise, Barak, and take captive your captives, son of Abinoam!
en.B: Wake up, wake up, Deborah! \q Wake up, wake up, break into song! \q Rise up, Barak, son of Abinoam, and lead your captives away!
en.R: Wake up, Deborah, wake up! \q Wake up and sing a song! \q Get up, Barak son of Abinoam! Lead away the prisoners you have taken!

decisions.choice: the song calls to Deborah and Barak, rousing them to lead the battle and the victory song
decisions.reason: Though Deborah is a singer of the song, it speaks to her and to Barak as its heroes. The doubled "awake" is a call to rise and act (Isaiah 51:9; 52:1).

decisions.choice: take captive your captives: lead away the prisoners you have taken, in triumph
decisions.reason: The verb and noun come from the same root. The picture is a victor leading his captives in procession (Psalm 68:19).

decisions.choice: break into song (Balanced); sing a song (Readable)
decisions.reason: The verb is "speak"; with "a song" it means to sing out.

source.text: אָ֚ז יְרַ֣ד שָׂרִ֔יד לְאַדִּירִ֖ים עָ֑ם יְהוָ֕ה יְרַד־לִ֖י בַּגִּבּוֹרִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: Then came down [the] survivor to nobles, [the] people; Yahweh came down for me against the mighty.

en.L: Then [the] survivors came down to [the] nobles, [the] people; \q {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} came down for me against the mighty.
en.B: Then the survivors came down, the people, to join the nobles; \q {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} came down for me against the mighty.
en.R: Then the people who were left came down to join their leaders. \q {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} came down to fight for me against the strong warriors.

decisions.choice: the people | the LORD came down for me: the LORD himself comes down to fight
alternatives: then the survivors came down to the nobles; the people of the LORD came down to me against the mighty
decisions.reason: The accents in the Hebrew text end the first line at "the people", so "the LORD" begins the second line as the subject of "came down". Without that division the words read "the people of the LORD came down for me against the mighty". The verse is very hard.

decisions.choice: came down: went down to the battle
alternatives: then he made the survivors rule over the nobles
decisions.reason: The vowels in the text are unusual. Read as the verb "go down", the line matches verses 11 and 14. Read as the verb "rule", it means "then he made the survivors rule over the nobles".

decisions.choice: survivors: those left after the years of oppression
decisions.reason: The word is used for those who escape or are left after disaster (Joshua 10:20). Israel was few and unarmed (verse 8).

decisions.choice: the mighty: the enemy's warriors
decisions.reason: The word means strong men, warriors; here it is the Canaanite army, as in verse 23.

decisions.choice: to fight for me
decisions.reason: Readable says why the LORD came down.

source.text: מִנִּ֣י אֶפְרַ֗יִם שָׁרְשָׁם֙ בַּעֲמָלֵ֔ק אַחֲרֶ֥יךָ בִנְיָמִ֖ין בַּֽעֲמָמֶ֑יךָ מִנִּ֣י מָכִ֗יר יָֽרְדוּ֙ מְחֹ֣קְקִ֔ים וּמִ֨זְּבוּלֻ֔ן מֹשְׁכִ֖ים בְּשֵׁ֥בֶט סֹפֵֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: From Ephraim [those whose] root [is] in Amalek; after you, Benjamin, with your peoples; from Machir came down commanders, and from Zebulun those holding with [the] staff of [the] scribe.

en.L: From Ephraim, [those whose] root [is] in Amalek; \q after you, Benjamin, with your kinsfolk; \q from Machir came down commanders, \q and from Zebulun those who hold the staff of [the] scribe.
en.B: From Ephraim came those whose roots are in Amalek; \q after you, Benjamin, they came among your people. \q From Machir came down commanders, \q and from Zebulun those who carry the officer's staff.
en.R: People came from Ephraim, from land where Amalek once lived. \q They followed Benjamin and his people. \q Commanders came down from Machir. \q Men came from Zebulun with the staff of the officer who calls up the army.

decisions.choice: from Ephraim, whose root is in Amalek: Ephraimites settled in land once linked with the Amalekites
alternatives: from Ephraim they set out into the valley
decisions.reason: Judges 12:15 speaks of "the hill country of the Amalekites" in Ephraim. The line is hard, and the ancient Greek translation has "in the valley" instead of "in Amalek", as in verse 15.

decisions.choice: after you, Benjamin: a battle cry; Benjamin led and Ephraim followed
decisions.reason: Hosea 5:8 has the same cry, "after you, Benjamin!" Benjamin lay next to Ephraim, near where Deborah judged (4:5).

decisions.choice: Machir: the clan of Manasseh
decisions.reason: Machir was the son of Manasseh (Numbers 32:39-40; Joshua 17:1). Here the name stands for Manasseh, as Gilead in verse 17 stands for Gad.

decisions.choice: the staff of the scribe: the staff of the officer who musters and records the troops
decisions.reason: The scribe kept the lists of men called to fight (2 Kings 25:19). Those who hold his staff are officers, so Zebulun sent leaders as well as men (4:6, 10).

decisions.choice: from land where Amalek once lived; men
decisions.reason: Readable explains the picture of a root in Amalek, and names the soldiers of Zebulun as men, as the fighters were.

source.text: וְשָׂרַ֤י בְּיִשָּׂשכָר֙ עִם־דְּבֹרָ֔ה וְיִשָּׂשכָר֙ כֵּ֣ן בָּרָ֔ק בָּעֵ֖מֶק שֻׁלַּ֣ח בְּרַגְלָ֑יו בִּפְלַגּ֣וֹת רְאוּבֵ֔ן גְּדֹלִ֖ים חִקְקֵי־לֵֽב׃

records.literal_gloss: And my commanders in Issachar [were] with Deborah, and Issachar so Barak; into the valley he was sent at his feet. Among [the] divisions of Reuben great [were the] resolves of heart.

en.L: And the commanders in Issachar [were] with Deborah, \q and Issachar [was] so [with] Barak; \q into the valley [they] were sent at his feet. \q Among the divisions of Reuben \q great [were the] resolves of heart.
en.B: The commanders of Issachar were with Deborah, \q and Issachar stood with Barak too, \q rushing into the valley at his heels. \q Among the divisions of Reuben \q there were great resolutions of heart.
en.R: The commanders of Issachar were with Deborah. \q Issachar stood with Barak and rushed after him into the valley. \q But the clans of Reuben only made big plans.

decisions.choice: the commanders of Issachar
decisions.reason: The ending on "commanders" can be read as "my" ("my commanders in Issachar") or as an old linking vowel ("the commanders of Issachar"). The sense is the same: Issachar's leaders came to fight.

decisions.choice: they were sent into the valley at his heels: they rushed down behind Barak into the plain
decisions.reason: Barak came down from Mount Tabor into the Jezreel Valley with his men behind him (4:14). "At his feet" means close behind him.

decisions.choice: great resolves of heart: Reuben made great decisions and plans
decisions.reason: The word means decrees or resolutions. Verse 16 repeats the line with a word differing by one letter, "searchings of heart": Reuben decided much and did nothing. Some Hebrew copies have the same word in both verses.

decisions.choice: Reuben: the tribe east of the Jordan, a people of flocks
decisions.reason: Reuben asked to settle east of the Jordan because of its many flocks (Numbers 32:1). The song now names the tribes that did not come (verses 15b-17).

decisions.choice: commanders
decisions.reason: The word is often "princes" or "leaders"; in this muster for battle it is the men who led Issachar's troops.

decisions.choice: only made big plans
decisions.reason: Readable says what the resolves of heart came to, as verse 16 shows.

source.text: לָ֣מָּה יָשַׁ֗בְתָּ בֵּ֚ין הַֽמִּשְׁפְּתַ֔יִם לִשְׁמֹ֖עַ שְׁרִק֣וֹת עֲדָרִ֑ים לִפְלַגּ֣וֹת רְאוּבֵ֔ן גְּדוֹלִ֖ים חִקְרֵי־לֵֽב׃

records.literal_gloss: Why did you sit between the sheepfolds, to hear whistlings of flocks? For [the] divisions of Reuben great [were the] searchings of heart.

en.L: Why did you sit among the sheepfolds, \q to hear the whistling for the flocks? \q For the divisions of Reuben \q great [were the] searchings of heart.
en.B: Why did you stay among the sheepfolds, \q listening to the shepherds whistling to their flocks? \q Among the divisions of Reuben \q there was great searching of heart.
en.R: Why did you stay home by the sheep pens \q and listen to the shepherds calling their flocks? \q The clans of Reuben could not make up their minds.

decisions.choice: the sheepfolds: the pens where flocks are kept
decisions.reason: The word has a dual form and is found only here and in Genesis 49:14, of Issachar. It may mean the walls of a sheepfold, the campfires, or the two saddlebags of a donkey. Each pictures staying at home with the animals.

decisions.choice: the whistling for the flocks: shepherds calling their sheep
decisions.reason: The word means whistling or piping; shepherds whistle or pipe to call and lead their flocks.

decisions.choice: "why did you sit?": a rebuke to Reuben for staying away
decisions.reason: The question is not asking for information. It blames Reuben, who talked much and stayed with the flocks while others risked their lives (verse 18).

decisions.choice: searchings of heart: much thinking, discussion and hesitating
decisions.reason: See verse 15. The changed word turns the great plans into endless questioning.

decisions.choice: could not make up their minds
decisions.reason: Readable says what "great searchings of heart" means.

source.text: גִּלְעָ֗ד בְּעֵ֤בֶר הַיַּרְדֵּן֙ שָׁכֵ֔ן וְדָ֕ן לָ֥מָּה יָג֖וּר אֳנִיּ֑וֹת אָשֵׁ֗ר יָשַׁב֙ לְח֣וֹף יַמִּ֔ים וְעַ֥ל מִפְרָצָ֖יו יִשְׁכּֽוֹן׃

records.literal_gloss: Gilead across the Jordan dwelt, and Dan, why does he sojourn [by] ships? Asher sat at [the] shore of [the] seas, and by his landings he dwells.

en.L: Gilead stayed across the Jordan; \q and Dan, why did he linger [by] ships? \q Asher sat at the shore of the seas, \q and stayed by his landing places.
en.B: Gilead stayed across the Jordan. \q And Dan, why did he linger by the ships? \q Asher sat still along the seacoast, \q settled by his harbors.
en.R: The people of Gilead stayed across the Jordan River. \q And why did the people of Dan stay with their ships? \q The tribe of Asher stayed by the sea \q and did not leave its harbors.

decisions.choice: Gilead: the land east of the Jordan, standing for the tribe of Gad
decisions.reason: Gad and half of Manasseh settled in Gilead (Numbers 32:1-5, 33-40; Joshua 13:24-31). Gad is not otherwise named in the song. Seen from the land west of the river, Gilead is across the Jordan.

decisions.choice: Dan by the ships: Dan, near the coast, stayed working with ships
decisions.reason: Dan's first land reached the coast near Joppa (Joshua 19:40-46), before the tribe moved north (chapter 18). The verb means to live as a guest or resident foreigner, so Danites may have worked on others' ships.

decisions.choice: his landing places: coves or inlets where boats come ashore
decisions.reason: The word is found only here; it comes from a verb meaning "break through", so it may mean the breaks in the coastline.

decisions.choice: the people of Gilead; the people of Dan; the tribe of Asher
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that the names stand for the tribes who lived there.

source.text: זְבֻל֗וּן עַ֣ם חֵרֵ֥ף נַפְשׁ֛וֹ לָמ֖וּת וְנַפְתָּלִ֑י עַ֖ל מְרוֹמֵ֥י שָׂדֶֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: Zebulun [was] a people [that] scorned its life to die, and Naphtali, on [the] heights of [the] field.

en.L: Zebulun [was] a people that scorned its life to [the] death, and Naphtali, \q on the heights of the field.
en.B: Zebulun was a people who held their lives cheap, ready to die, and so was Naphtali, \q on the high ground of the open field.
en.R: But the people of Zebulun and Naphtali risked their lives. \q They were ready to die fighting on the high fields.

decisions.choice: scorned its life to death: risked their lives, ready to die
decisions.reason: The verb means to treat with scorn; to scorn one's own life is to count it as nothing and face death without holding back.

decisions.choice: Zebulun and Naphtali: the two tribes Barak first called
decisions.reason: Barak gathered men from Zebulun and Naphtali at Mount Tabor (4:6, 10). The song sets their courage against the tribes that stayed home (verses 15-17).

decisions.choice: the heights of the field: the high ground of the open country
decisions.reason: This may be Mount Tabor and the slopes above the valley, or the field of battle itself.

decisions.choice: the people of Zebulun and Naphtali; but
decisions.reason: Readable puts the two tribes together and marks the contrast with the tribes in verses 15-17.

source.text: בָּ֤אוּ מְלָכִים֙ נִלְחָ֔מוּ אָ֤ז נִלְחֲמוּ֙ מַלְכֵ֣י כְנַ֔עַן בְּתַעְנַ֖ךְ עַל־מֵ֣י מְגִדּ֑וֹ בֶּ֥צַע כֶּ֖סֶף לֹ֥א לָקָֽחוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: Came kings, they fought; then fought [the] kings of Canaan at Taanach by [the] waters of Megiddo; gain of silver not they took.

en.L: Kings came, they fought; \q then the kings of Canaan fought, \q at Taanach, by the waters of Megiddo; \q gain of silver they did not take.
en.B: The kings came and fought; \q the kings of Canaan fought then, \q at Taanach, by the streams of Megiddo, \q but they carried off no silver as plunder.
en.R: Kings came and fought. \q The kings of Canaan fought \q at Taanach, near the streams of Megiddo. \q But they did not take home any silver.

decisions.choice: Taanach and the waters of Megiddo: Canaanite towns on the south side of the Jezreel Valley, near the Kishon
decisions.reason: Both towns guarded the passes into the valley (Joshua 12:21; 17:11). The waters of Megiddo are the streams there that feed the Kishon (verse 21).

decisions.choice: kings of Canaan: Jabin's allies, the kings who fought with Sisera
decisions.reason: Chapter 4 names Jabin, king of Canaan, and his commander Sisera (4:2). Other city kings joined them.

decisions.choice: gain of silver they did not take: they won no plunder
decisions.reason: They came hoping for spoil (verse 30) and went away with nothing.

decisions.choice: the streams of Megiddo
decisions.reason: "Waters" here are the streams that run near the town.

source.text: מִן־שָׁמַ֖יִם נִלְחָ֑מוּ הַכּֽוֹכָבִים֙ מִמְּסִלּוֹתָ֔ם נִלְחֲמ֖וּ עִם־סִיסְרָֽא׃

records.literal_gloss: From heaven they fought, the stars from their courses fought with Sisera.

en.L: From heaven they fought; \q the stars from their courses \q fought against Sisera.
en.B: From the heavens the fight was joined; \q the stars, along their courses, \q made war on Sisera.
en.R: The stars in the sky joined the battle. \q As they moved along their paths, \q they fought against Sisera.

decisions.choice: the stars fought from heaven: the powers of heaven fought on Israel's side
decisions.reason: The stars are the LORD's host or army (Isaiah 40:26). The song pictures heaven itself joining the battle, as in the storm of verses 4 and 21 and the hailstones of Joshua 10:11. It does not teach that the stars rule events; they serve the LORD.

decisions.choice: their courses: the paths the stars travel across the sky
decisions.reason: The word means a raised road or highway (20:31-32).

decisions.choice: the fight was joined
decisions.reason: The verb "they fought" has the stars as its subject; Balanced keeps "from the heavens" first, as the Hebrew does.

source.text: נַ֤חַל קִישׁוֹן֙ גְּרָפָ֔ם נַ֥חַל קְדוּמִ֖ים נַ֣חַל קִישׁ֑וֹן תִּדְרְכִ֥י נַפְשִׁ֖י עֹֽז׃

records.literal_gloss: [The] torrent of Kishon swept them away, [the] torrent of ancient days, [the] torrent of Kishon; you will tread, my soul, strength!

en.L: The torrent Kishon swept them away, \q the ancient torrent, the torrent Kishon. \q March on, my soul, [in] strength!
en.B: The Kishon River swept them off, \q the age-old river, the Kishon River. \q My soul, march on in strength!
en.R: The Kishon River swept them away, \q that very old river, the Kishon. \q March on, my soul, and be strong!

decisions.choice: the torrent Kishon: a stream that floods in the rainy season
decisions.reason: The word names a valley with a stream that can rise fast in heavy rain. The Kishon runs through the Jezreel Valley past Megiddo (4:7, 13). The storm of verse 4 flooded it and swept the enemy away.

decisions.choice: ancient: a river from long ago
decisions.reason: The word means "from ancient times". Others take it from the verb "come to meet", giving "the onrushing torrent" or "the torrent of battles".

decisions.choice: march on, my soul, in strength: the singer urges herself on
alternatives: you trampled the strong, my soul
decisions.reason: The verb is addressed to "my soul", that is, the singer's own self. The last word may also be the object: "my soul, you trod down the strong", the singer tramples the enemy. The line is hard.

decisions.choice: the Kishon River
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable call the stream a river, the familiar English word for it.

source.text: אָ֥ז הָלְמ֖וּ עִקְּבֵי־ס֑וּס מִֽדַּהֲר֖וֹת דַּהֲר֥וֹת אַבִּירָֽיו׃

records.literal_gloss: Then hammered [the] heels of [the] horse from gallopings, gallopings of his mighty ones.

en.L: Then the hoofs of [the] horses hammered, \q from the galloping, galloping of his mighty ones.
en.B: Then the horses' hoofs hammered the ground \q as his strong steeds galloped and galloped.
en.R: Then the horses' hoofs pounded the ground \q as the strong war horses galloped on and on.

decisions.choice: his mighty ones: his strong horses, stallions
decisions.reason: The word means "mighty" and is used of strong horses in Jeremiah 8:16 and 47:3. "His" most likely means Sisera's, whose chariot horses fled. It could also mean the warriors themselves.

decisions.choice: galloping, galloping: the repeated word imitates the sound of hoofs
decisions.reason: The doubled word, with its many repeated sounds, makes the hearer hear the horses pounding in flight.

decisions.choice: the ground
decisions.reason: "Hammered" has no object; Balanced and Readable say what the hoofs struck.

source.text: א֣וֹרוּ מֵר֗וֹז אָמַר֙ מַלְאַ֣ךְ יְהוָ֔ה אֹ֥רוּ אָר֖וֹר יֹשְׁבֶ֑יהָ כִּ֤י לֹֽא־בָ֨אוּ֙ לְעֶזְרַ֣ת יְהוָ֔ה לְעֶזְרַ֥ת יְהוָ֖ה בַּגִּבּוֹרִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: Curse Meroz, says [the] angel of Yahweh, curse, cursing, its inhabitants, for not they came to [the] help of Yahweh, to [the] help of Yahweh against the mighty.

en.L: 'Curse Meroz,' says the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, \q 'curse bitterly its inhabitants, \q for they did not come to the help of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, \q to the help of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} against the mighty.'
en.B: 'Curse Meroz,' says the angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}; \q 'curse its people bitterly, \q because they did not come to help {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, \q to stand with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} against the warriors.'
en.R: The angel of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says, 'Curse the town of Meroz! \q Put a terrible curse on the people who live there! \q They did not come to help {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. \q They did not help {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} fight the strong warriors.'

decisions.choice: Meroz: a town near the battle, otherwise unknown
decisions.reason: Meroz is not named anywhere else. It seems to have been an Israelite town that could have helped and did not.

decisions.choice: the angel of the LORD: the LORD's messenger, speaking with his authority
decisions.reason: On who the angel of the LORD is, see the note at 2:1. Here he speaks the curse on those who refused to fight.

decisions.choice: curse bitterly: the verb is repeated with an infinitive for force
decisions.reason: Hebrew strengthens a verb by adding its own infinitive; the curse is to be complete.

decisions.choice: to the help of the LORD: to fight on the LORD's side
decisions.reason: The battle is the LORD's (verses 4-5, 13, 20). Not coming to help Israel was refusing to help the LORD.

decisions.choice: single quotation marks
decisions.reason: The angel's words are quoted inside the song, which is itself a quotation.

source.text: תְּבֹרַךְ֙ מִנָּשִׁ֔ים יָעֵ֕ל אֵ֖שֶׁת חֶ֣בֶר הַקֵּינִ֑י מִנָּשִׁ֥ים בָּאֹ֖הֶל תְּבֹרָֽךְ׃

records.literal_gloss: May she be blessed above women, Jael, [the] wife of Heber the Kenite; above women in the tent may she be blessed.

en.L: May Jael be blessed above women, \q the wife of Heber the Kenite; \q above women in the tent may she be blessed.
en.B: May Jael be blessed above all women, \q the wife of Heber the Kenite, \q blessed above all women who live in tents.
en.R: May Jael be blessed more than all other women, \q Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite! \q Of all women who live in tents, may she be blessed the most.

decisions.choice: may she be blessed above women: a wish and praise, that she be the most blessed of women
decisions.reason: The verb can be a wish ("may she be blessed") or a statement ("she is most blessed"). "From women" compares her with them: more than other women. The same word, "blessed", ends the line, framing it.

decisions.choice: Heber the Kenite; women in the tent: Jael belonged to a people who lived in tents
decisions.reason: The Kenites were related to Moses' father-in-law and lived in tents among Israel (1:16; 4:11, 17). The tent is also where she killed Sisera (4:17-21); it stands in contrast with the window of Sisera's mother (verse 28).

decisions.choice: Jael (repeated)
decisions.reason: Readable names Jael again so that the second line stands as its own phrase.

source.text: מַ֥יִם שָׁאַ֖ל חָלָ֣ב נָתָ֑נָה בְּסֵ֥פֶל אַדִּירִ֖ים הִקְרִ֥יבָה חֶמְאָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: Water he asked; milk she gave; in [a] bowl of nobles she brought curds.

en.L: Water he asked; milk she gave; \q in a bowl of nobles she brought curds.
en.B: He asked for water, and she gave milk; \q she served him curds in a bowl fit for princes.
en.R: Sisera asked for water, but she gave him milk. \q She brought him rich curdled milk in a bowl fit for royalty.

decisions.choice: milk and curds: rich milk, more than he asked for
decisions.reason: Curds are thick soured milk or cream, a fine thing to give a guest (Genesis 18:8). In 4:19 she opens a skin of milk. Her generous welcome puts him off guard.

decisions.choice: a bowl of nobles: a large, fine bowl, fit for important guests
decisions.reason: The word for the bowl is used again only in 6:38, for a bowl that holds much water.

decisions.choice: Sisera
decisions.reason: Readable names the man who asked.

source.text: יָדָהּ֙ לַיָּתֵ֣ד תִּשְׁלַ֔חְנָה וִֽימִינָ֖הּ לְהַלְמ֣וּת עֲמֵלִ֑ים וְהָלְמָ֤ה סִֽיסְרָא֙ מָחֲקָ֣ה רֹאשׁ֔וֹ וּמָחֲצָ֥ה וְחָלְפָ֖ה רַקָּתֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: Her hand to [the] tent peg she stretched out, and her right hand to [the] hammer of laborers; and she hammered Sisera, she crushed his head, and she shattered and she pierced his temple.

en.L: Her hand she stretched out to the tent peg, \q and her right hand to the laborers' hammer; \q and she hammered Sisera, she crushed his head, \q she shattered and pierced his temple.
en.B: She reached out her hand for the tent peg, \q her right hand for the workman's mallet. \q She struck Sisera and crushed his head; \q she broke through and pierced his temple.
en.R: She took a tent peg in one hand \q and a heavy hammer in her right hand. \q She hit Sisera and crushed his head. \q She drove the peg right through the side of his head.

decisions.choice: the tent peg and the laborers' hammer: the tools used to put up a tent
decisions.reason: Among tent-dwelling peoples, women often pitched the tents, so these were tools Jael knew well (4:21).

decisions.choice: she stretched out: the verb has an unusual form
decisions.reason: The form looks plural, but it has her hand as its subject; it may be an old or poetic form. The sense is clear.

decisions.choice: struck, crushed, shattered, pierced: one blow told with four verbs
decisions.reason: The verb "crush" is found only here. The heaping up of verbs slows the moment and shows the force of the blow to his temple, the side of the head above the ear (4:21-22).

decisions.choice: drove the peg right through the side of his head
decisions.reason: Readable says what pierced his temple, as 4:21 tells, and explains "temple".

source.text: בֵּ֣ין רַגְלֶ֔יהָ כָּרַ֥ע נָפַ֖ל שָׁכָ֑ב בֵּ֤ין רַגְלֶ֨יהָ֙ כָּרַ֣ע נָפָ֔ל בַּאֲשֶׁ֣ר כָּרַ֔ע שָׁ֖ם נָפַ֥ל שָׁדֽוּד׃

records.literal_gloss: Between her feet he bowed, he fell, he lay; between her feet he bowed, he fell; in where he bowed, there he fell, destroyed.

en.L: Between her feet he sank, he fell, he lay; \q between her feet he sank, he fell; \q where he sank, there he fell, destroyed.
en.B: At her feet he sank down, he fell, he lay still; \q at her feet he sank down, he fell; \q at the place where he sank down, there he fell, slain.
en.R: He sank down at her feet. \q He fell and lay there at her feet. \q Right where he sank down, he fell dead.

decisions.choice: between her feet: at her feet; he collapsed before her
decisions.reason: The picture is of a defeated enemy brought down at the feet of the one who struck him (2 Samuel 22:39). The mighty commander falls before a woman (4:9).

decisions.choice: sank, fell, lay: he went down on his knees, fell over and lay still
decisions.reason: The first verb means to bend the knees or sink down. The poem pictures his fall in slow repeated steps. Chapter 4 tells that he was asleep when she struck him (4:21); the song paints his collapse without that detail.

decisions.choice: destroyed: dead, done for
decisions.reason: The word means "ruined" or "destroyed", and here describes him lying dead.

decisions.choice: slain
decisions.reason: Balanced uses a word that says he was killed, not merely ruined.

source.text: בְּעַד֩ הַחַלּ֨וֹן נִשְׁקְפָ֧ה וַתְּיַבֵּ֛ב אֵ֥ם סִֽיסְרָ֖א בְּעַ֣ד הָֽאֶשְׁנָ֑ב מַדּ֗וּעַ בֹּשֵׁ֤שׁ רִכְבּוֹ֙ לָב֔וֹא מַדּ֣וּעַ אֶֽחֱר֔וּ פַּעֲמֵ֖י מַרְכְּבוֹתָֽיו׃

records.literal_gloss: Through the window she looked down, and she cried out, [the] mother of Sisera, through the lattice: why is ashamed his chariot to come? Why do they delay, [the] steps of his chariots?

en.L: Through the window she looked down, \q and the mother of Sisera cried out through the lattice: \q 'Why is his chariot slow to come? \q Why do the hoofbeats of his chariots delay?'
en.B: Through the window she looked out, \q Sisera's mother, and cried through the lattice, \q 'Why is his chariot taking so long to come? \q Why are the hoofbeats of his chariots so late?'
en.R: Sisera's mother looked out through the window. \q She cried out through the lattice, \q 'Why is his chariot so slow to come home? \q Why do I not hear the sound of his chariot horses?'

decisions.choice: cried out: called out shrilly or wailed
decisions.reason: The verb is found only here. In related languages it means to cry out loud or to lament.

decisions.choice: the window and the lattice: a window screened with woodwork in a fine house
decisions.reason: Sisera's mother waits in a palace, watching for her son's return, while he lies dead in a tent (verse 27).

decisions.choice: slow, delayed: the chariots are long in coming
decisions.reason: The first verb usually means "be ashamed"; with a following verb it means to be slow or late (Exodus 32:1). The "steps" of the chariots are the beat of their horses' hoofs.

decisions.choice: single quotation marks
decisions.reason: Her words are quoted inside the song.

source.text: חַכְמ֥וֹת שָׂרוֹתֶ֖יהָ תַּעֲנֶ֑ינָּה אַף־הִ֕יא תָּשִׁ֥יב אֲמָרֶ֖יהָ לָֽהּ׃

records.literal_gloss: [The] wise of her ladies answer her; indeed she returns her words to herself:

en.L: The wisest of her ladies answer her; \q indeed, she returns her words to herself:
en.B: The wisest of her noble ladies answer her; \q she even gives herself the same answer:
en.R: Her wisest ladies give her an answer, \q and she keeps telling herself the same thing:

decisions.choice: her wisest ladies: the noblewomen of her household
decisions.reason: The word for the ladies is the feminine of the word for princes or officials. The "wise" ones are about to give a confident answer that is wrong, which makes them the object of the song's irony.

decisions.choice: she returns her words to herself: she repeats their answer to herself
decisions.reason: To "return words" is to answer. She tells herself what her ladies say, or gives herself her own answer, to calm her fear. The words of verse 30 are that answer.

source.text: הֲלֹ֨א יִמְצְא֜וּ יְחַלְּק֣וּ שָׁלָ֗ל רַ֤חַם רַחֲמָתַ֨יִם֙ לְרֹ֣אשׁ גֶּ֔בֶר שְׁלַ֤ל צְבָעִים֙ לְסִ֣יסְרָ֔א שְׁלַ֥ל צְבָעִ֖ים רִקְמָ֑ה צֶ֥בַע רִקְמָתַ֖יִם לְצַוְּארֵ֥י שָׁלָֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: Are not they finding, dividing spoil? A womb, two wombs for [the] head of [a] man; spoil of dyed cloths for Sisera, spoil of dyed cloths, embroidery, dyed cloth, two embroideries for [the] necks of spoil?

en.L: 'Are they not finding [and] dividing spoil? \q a womb, two wombs for [the] head of each man; \q spoil of dyed cloths for Sisera, \q spoil of dyed cloths, embroidered, \q dyed cloth, doubly embroidered, for [the] necks of [the] spoil?'
en.B: 'They must be finding the spoil and sharing it out: \q a girl or two for every man; \q colored cloth as spoil for Sisera, \q colored cloth as spoil, richly embroidered, \q dyed cloth embroidered on both sides, for necks among the spoil.'
en.R: 'They must be finding things to take and sharing them out. \q Each soldier gets a girl or two. \q Sisera gets fine colored cloth, cloth with fancy stitching, \q scarves with fancy stitching on both sides to wear around the neck.'

decisions.choice: a womb, two wombs: a girl or two for each soldier, taken as captives
decisions.reason: The word "womb" is crude soldiers' talk for captured women. The cruel irony is that she pictures her son taking Israelite women, while he lies dead at the feet of an Israelite woman's ally (verse 27).

decisions.choice: dyed cloths, embroidery: costly colored and embroidered fabric
decisions.reason: Dyed and embroidered cloth was valuable plunder. The dual form may mean two pieces of embroidery or cloth embroidered on both sides.

decisions.choice: for the necks of the spoil: pieces to be worn around the neck, taken as spoil
alternatives: for the necks of the plunderers
decisions.reason: The phrase is hard. As written it seems to mean necks among the spoil, or the necks of those who take the spoil. A small change in the letters gives "for my neck as spoil", the mother hoping for a gift for herself.

decisions.choice: "are they not finding?": a question that expects "yes"
decisions.reason: The ladies answer with confidence: surely the army is late because it is dividing the plunder.

decisions.choice: a girl or two
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense of "a womb, two wombs"; Literal keeps the crude word.

decisions.choice: scarves to wear around the neck
decisions.reason: Readable reads the cloth for the neck as scarves.

source.text: כֵּ֠ן יֹאבְד֤וּ כָל־אוֹיְבֶ֨יךָ֙ יְהוָ֔ה וְאֹ֣הֲבָ֔יו כְּצֵ֥את הַשֶּׁ֖מֶשׁ בִּגְבֻרָת֑וֹ וַתִּשְׁקֹ֥ט הָאָ֖רֶץ אַרְבָּעִ֥ים שָׁנָֽה׃פ

records.literal_gloss: So may they perish, all your enemies, Yahweh, and [those] loving him [be] like [the] going out of the sun in its might. And was quiet the land forty years.

en.L: So may all {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} enemies perish, O {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, \q and those who love {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} [be] like the going out of the sun in its might!" \q And the land was quiet forty years.
en.B: So may all {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} enemies perish, {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}! \q But may those who love {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} be like the sun as it rises in its strength." \q And the land had peace for forty years.
en.R: {{divine_name:LORD|Yahweh}}, may all {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} enemies die like this! \q But may those who love {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} shine like the sun when it rises in all its strength." \q Then the land had peace for forty years.

decisions.choice: so may they perish: may all the LORD's enemies end as Sisera did
decisions.reason: "So" points back to Sisera's death and his mother's vain waiting. The song closes with a prayer.

decisions.choice: your enemies ... those who love him: the song turns from speaking to the LORD to speaking about him
decisions.reason: Hebrew poetry often moves between "you" and "he" in speaking of God (Psalm 23:2-4). Both mean the LORD.

decisions.choice: like the sun rising in its might: growing brighter and stronger, like the sun at dawn
decisions.reason: The sun is pictured as a strong man going out to run his course (Psalm 19:6). Those who love the LORD rise in strength, while his enemies fall.

decisions.choice: the last sentence is the narrator's, not part of the song
decisions.reason: "And the land was quiet forty years" closes the account of Deborah, as the same words close the stories of earlier judges (3:11, 30). The song ends before it.

decisions.choice: the song's double quotation mark closes before "And the land"; the narrator's sentence is set as a line of its own
decisions.reason: Verse 31 holds both the end of the song and the narrator's closing words; the closing quote marks where the song ends.

decisions.choice: shine (Readable)
decisions.reason: Readable says what it means to be like the rising sun: to shine with growing strength.
